lines: A real burst of requests, all arriving at once, hits a service whose own door can only hold so much waiting work before something has to be turned away.
Once it all settles, is every single one of those requests accounted for, either let through or turned away?
answer: Nothing just vanishes. Every one lands on one side or the other.

lines: Run it for real: of the whole real burst, exactly half get let through, and exactly half get turned away, and every single one is accounted for as one or the other.
Look specifically at the ones that got turned away.
Could any one of those have actually arrived earlier than one of the ones that got let through?
answer: Every one that gets turned away arrives after every one that gets let through, never mixed in.

lines: Run it for real: every single one turned away genuinely arrived after every single one let through. It's a clean split by arrival, never an arbitrary pick.
steps.takeaway: A door that's genuinely full turns away whatever shows up next, not some arbitrary pick from everyone who arrived.

lines: The identical real burst is run again, from a brand new copy of the same service.
Does it come back with the identical split, or does real timing just happen to shuffle things differently this time?
answer: There's enough real room on either side of that line that ordinary timing noise can't move it.

lines: Run it for real: run again from scratch, the identical split comes back exactly, confirming this is real, dependable behavior, not something that happened to go one way by chance the first time.
steps.takeaway: Something that doesn't come back the same way twice can't be judged against a real, stated limit at all.

lines: One real, independent page, and a second real, independent page right beside it, each describe one of these two exact ideas, in their own words.

One describes turning away work once whatever's handling it genuinely isn't ready for more. The other describes setting an explicit, agreed number for how much of that turning-away is actually allowed before it counts as a real problem.
steps.takeaway: An explicit, stated limit is what turns a measured rate of turned-away work into an expected, judged cost instead of an unexplained problem.

lines: So here's what this topic's own two real runs are really standing in for: once a real door is genuinely full, it turns away whatever shows up next, cleanly, by arrival, never by some arbitrary pick.
And that exact rate, measured the same way twice, comes back the same both times, which is exactly what makes it something you can actually set a real, honest limit against.
Without that stated limit, the identical, dependable number looks like an unexplained problem instead of what it actually is: a resource behaving exactly as expected under real pressure.
